Claudia Doblinger (TU Munich). The manuscript covers the full argument, all methodological choices
with their justifications and citations, the complete results with robustness tables, the
carbon-capture case study, limitations, and a statement on how AI tools were used to build the
project.

## Abstract

Science and technology has advanced to the point where we can treat DNA as a programming language
and living organisms as hardware. With standardized genetic parts and widely used assembly
protocols, life itself has become a series of tools to optimize production. This project studies
different forms of research in synthetic biology, student projects, academic publications, and
patents, to see if geography plays a role in determining the focus of research.

Are students, academics, and private industry researching the same topics in the cities they live
and work? The International Genetically Engineered Machine competition, iGEM, is a nonprofit that
advances synthetic biology education through an annual student research competition, and its data
is a wealth of insight into how the field innovates. We compare the corpus of iGEM projects against
academic publications and patents to test whether geographically-influenced semantic relatedness can
be established. Relatedness between iGEM projects, academic research, and patent abstracts is
calculated, established, and empirically tested. Clusters are identified in the semantic space, and
those related to carbon capture are inspected in depth. The research landscapes of cities are
compared, and policy suggestions are made.

## What the thesis argues

The project builds a corpus that did not exist, 17,826 geocoded artifacts across three artifact
types, embeds them in one fine-tuned semantic space, and tests whether a city's projects, papers,
and patents share specific topics more than chance allows.

- A naive centroid measure of city alignment is a size artifact and is discarded.
- A topic co-membership measure, tested against a within-country permutation null, shows real,
  size-independent local relatedness between a city's projects and papers, and between its papers
  and patents.
- The direct project-to-patent link never reaches significance: the field is shaped like a star with
  papers at the hub, not a triangle.
- The pattern survives dropping any country, changing the cluster resolution, varying the depth
  threshold, and using the base embedding model before any fine-tuning.
- It is anchored outside the language model entirely: a Mantel test finds that the mix of physical
  BioBrick parts a city's students build agrees with its semantic topic profile.
- The result is descriptive. It documents relatedness and co-location; it does not identify a causal
  mechanism.
